chapters.title: Chapter 0 : 모든 문법 및 표현 정리
Chapter 1 : what are you reading? -the train
chapters.locationNote: The train is en route from Budapest, Hungary, to Vienna, Austria.

lines.text: We see a middle-aged couple sitting in the front of the coach car. Celine is sitting across the aisle from them, reading a book. Jesse is reading a book as well.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.direction: Still looking in Celine’s direction; Points toward the exit
lines.text: Do you have any idea what they were arguing about?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Glances up at him, looks over

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Do you... do you speak English?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah. No, I'm sorry, my German is not very good.
Jesse leans back, disappointed. Celine pauses for a second, then continues.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Have you ever heard that as couples get older, they lose their ability to hear each other?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: No.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Well, supposedly, men lose the ability to hear higher-pitched sounds, and women eventually lose hearing in the low end. I guess they sort of nullify each other, or something.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I guess. Nature's way of allowing couples to grow old together without killing each other.
Celine smiles, small laugh, turns away.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: What are you reading?
She shows him.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Oh, yeah.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: How bout you?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.direction: Looks down, then laughs as he shows her, and she smiles.
lines.text: Umm.
Couple returns to car, still arguing, albeit a lot calmer.

lines.speaker: Woman
lines.text: Typisch! Sind ihre? Wirklich so gehuepft, dass du sie dauernd anstarren musst?
lines.translation: Typical! Are hers? Really jumped so much that you have to stare at her constantly?

lines.speaker: Man
lines.text: Vergiss es.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Look, I was thinking about going to the lounge car sometime soon. Would you like to come with me?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Okay.
They get up and leave the coach car. Jesse 'punches' the automated door mechanism as they enter the lounge car.

chapters.title: Chatper 2 : You’re American? Are you sure? - the Lounge Car
chapters.locationNote: The train continues en route from Budapest, Hungary, to Vienna, Austria.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: So how do you speak such good English?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: I went to school for a summer in Los Angeles. (Points to table) This fine here?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah, this is good.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Then I spent some time in London. How do you speak such good English?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Me? I'm American.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: You're American?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Are you sure?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: No, I'm joking. I knew you were American. And of course, you don't speak any other language, right?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah, yeah, I get it. So I'm the crude, dumb, vulgar American who has no culture, right? But, I tried. I took French for four years in high school. When I first got to Paris, I stood in line at the metro station. I was practicing. (Gestures with his hand to show how hard he was trying) “Une billet, s'il vous plaît. Une billet s'il vous plait…” (One ticket please. One ticket please…) You know…

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: UN billet.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Un. Whatever. Un, Un. (Laughs) Un billet s'il vous plaît, un billet s'il vous plaît, you know, and I get up there, and, uh, I look at this woman, and my mind goes completely blank. And I start saying, “Uh, listen, uh I need a ticket to get to...” you know, so anyway. (Pauses and swallows, before breaking the slience) So, where are you headed?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Well, back to Paris. My classes start next week.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Oh, you're still in school? Where do you go?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah, La Sorbonne, you know?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Well, sure. (Pause) Hey, you coming from Budapest?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah, I was visiting my grandmother.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Oh. How's she?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: She's okay.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: She's alright?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: She's fine, yeah. (Pause) How about you? Where are you going?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Uh, I'm going to Vienna.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Vienna? What's there?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Uh, I have no idea. I'm flying out of there tomorrow.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Aha. You on holiday?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Uh, ye- (Indecisive) Uh, I don't really know what I'm on.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Okay.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I've just been. I'm just traveling around. I've been riding the trains the past two, three weeks.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: You were visiting friends, or just on your own?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Uh, yeah. You know I had a friend in Madrid, but, umm...

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Madrid? That's nice.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah, I got one of those Eurail passes, is what I did.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: That's great. So, has this trip, around Europe, been good for you?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah, sure, yeah, it's been, umm...it sucked. You know...

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: What?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: No, uh, it's had its, umm. Well, I'll tell ya, you know, sitting, you know, for weeks on end, looking out the window has actually been kinda great.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: What do you mean?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Well, you know, for instance, you have ideas that you ordinarily wouldn't have.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: What kind of ideas?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: You want to hear one?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah, tell me.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Alright, uh, I had this idea, okay?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Um-hmm...

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: For a television show. Some friends of mine are these cable access producers, do you know what that is, cable access? (Céline shakes her head) Umm, I dunno...Anybody can produce a show real cheap, and they have to put it on. Right? And I have this idea for this show that would last twenty-four hours a day for a year straight, right? What you do, is you get three hundred and sixty-four people from cities all over the world, to do these twenty-four hour documents of real time, right, capturing life as it‘s lived. Um, you know, it would start with uh, a guy waking up in the morning, and, uh, you know, taking the long shower, eating a little breakfast, making a little coffee, you know, and, uh, reading the paper.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Wait, wait. All those mundane, boring things everybody has to do every day of their fucking life?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I was going to say the poetry of day to day life, but (Celine starts laughing) you know, you say the way you say it, I'll say it the way I say it...

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: I like that.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: No listen, think about it like this...

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Who's gonna want to watch this?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Well, alright, think about it like this. Why is it, that a dog, you know, sleeping in the sun, is so beautiful? You know, it is, it‘s beautiful, you know, but a guy, standing at a bank machine, trying to take some money out, looks like a complete moron?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: So, it‘s like a National Geographic program, but on people?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah!

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Hmm.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: What do you think?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah, I can. (Laughs) I can. (Laughs) I can see it. Like twenty-four boring hours, sorry, and like a three minute sex scene, where he falls asleep right after, no?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah, you know I mean, and...I mean, that would be a GREAT episode.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: People would talk about that episode. I mean, you and your friends could do one in Paris, if you wanted to, I mean.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Oh, sure.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I dunno, the key, the key (squints his eyes as if perplexed)...the thing that kind of haunts me is the distribution, you know. I mean, getting these tapes from town to town, city to city, so that the play is continuous, ‘cause it would have to play all the time, or else it just wouldn't work.
Waiter approaches the table, hands them menus

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Thanks. (Pause, while waiter walks away. The camera begins to pan out, as his voice fades out) You know what? Not service-oriented. It‘s just, I don't know, an observation about Europe.
Scene fades, then returns to lounge car an unknown amount of time later

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: You know my parents have never really spoken of the possibility of my falling in love, or getting married, or having children. Even as a little girl, they wanted me to think of a future career, as a, you know, as an interior designer, or a lawyer, or something like that. I'd say to my dad, “I want to be a writer.” and he'd say, “journalist.” I'd say I wanted to have a refuge for stray cats, and he'd say, “veterinarian.” I'd say I wanted to be an actress, and he'd say, “TV newscaster.” It was this constant conversion of my fanciful ambition into these practical, money-making ventures.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Hmm. I always had a pretty good bullshit detector when I was a kid, you know. I always knew when they were lying to me, you know? By the time I was in high school, I was dead set on listening to what everybody thought I should be doing with my life, and just kind of (shakes head, shrugs shoulders) doing just the opposite.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Mm-hmm.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: No one was ever mean about it. It‘s just, I could never get very excited about other people's ambitions for my life.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: But you know what, if your parents never really fully contradict you about anything, and like are basically nice, and supportive...

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Right...

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: It makes it even harder to officially complain. You know, even when they're wrong, it‘s this, it‘s this passive-aggressive shit, you know what I mean, it‘s... I hate it, I really hate it.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Well, you know, despite all that kind of bullshit that comes along with it, I remember childhood as this, you know, this magical time. I do. I remember when, uh, my mother first told me about death. My great-grandmother had just died, and my whole family had just visited them in Florida. I was about three, three and a half years old. Anyway, I was in the backyard, playing, and my sister had just taught me how to take the garden hose, and do it in such a way that, uh, (holds his hand up to demonstrate the garden hose technique) you could spray it into the sun, and you could make a rainbow. And so I was doing that, and through the mist, I could see my grandmother. And she was just standing there, smiling at me. And uh, then I held it there, for a long time, and I looked at her. And then finally, I let go of the nozzle, you know, and then I dropped the hose, and she disappeared. And so I went back inside, and I tell my parents, you know. And they, uh, sit me down give me big rap on how [when people die] you never see them again, and how I'd imagined it. But…I knew what I'd seen. And I was just glad that I saw that. I mean, I've never seen anything like that since. But, I don't know. It just kind of let me know how ambiguous everything was, you know, even death.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: You're really lucky you can have this attitude towards death. I think I'm afraid of death twenty-four hours a day. I swear. I mean, that's why I'm in a train right now. I could have flown to Paris, but I'm too scared.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Oh, come…

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: I can't help it. I can't help it. I know the statistics say na-na-na, it‘s safer, whatever. (Jesse laughs) When I'm in a plane, I can see it. I can see the explosion, (Jesse makes an explosion sound effect) I can see me falling through the clouds, and I'm so scared of those few seconds of consciousness before you're gonna die, you know, when you know for sure you're gonna die. I can't stop thinking that way. It‘s exhausting.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah, I bet.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Really exhausting. (She looks out window and points, as the train slows down) I think this is Vienna.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: You get off here, no?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah, what a drag. I wish I had met you earlier, you know, I really like talking to you.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah, me too. It was really nice to meet you.
Train stops, scene fades.

lines.text: He's so cute. (Sees a cemetery.) I visited this as a young teenager. I think it left a bigger impression on me at that time than any of the museums we went to.

lines.text: I think some were from accidents, on boats and things like that, but most of them were suicides that jumped in the river. lines.text: But you know what?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: What?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: I don't think it really matters what generation you are born into. Look at my parents. They were these angry, young, May '68 people, revolting against everything. You know, the government, their conservative catholic backgrounds, I mean. I was born not long after, and then my father went on to become this successful architect, and they began to travel all around the world, where he built bridges, and towers, and stuff. I mean, I really can't complain about anything. You know, they love me more than anything in the world, and I have been raised with all the freedom they had fought for. And yet for me now, it‘s another type of fight. We still have to deal with the same old shit, but we can't really know who, or you know, what the enemy is.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I don't really know if there is an enemy. You know, I mean, everybody's parents fuck them up. You know, rich kids' parents gave them too much, poor kids' not enough. Too much attention, not enough attention. They either left them, or you know, they stuck around and taught 'em the wrong things. You know. I mean, my parents are just these two people who didn't like each other very much, who, uh, decided to get married and have a kid, and they try their best to be nice to me.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Did your parents divorce?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah. Finally. They should have done it a lot sooner, but they stuck together for a while (in a prim “high-society” accent) for the well-being of my sister and I, thank you very much. (Back to normal voice.) I remember my mother once. She told me, right in front of my father, they were having this big fight, that he didn't really want to have me, you know, that he was really pissed off when he found out that she was pregnant with me, you know, that I was this big mistake. And I think that really shaped the way I think. I always saw the world as this place where I really wasn't meant to be.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: That's so sad.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: No, I mean, I eventually kind of took pride in it. You know, like my life was my own doing, or something. You know, like I was crashing 'The Big Party.’

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: That's a way to see it. You know, my parents, they're still married, and I guess they're very happy, but I just think it‘s a healthy process to rebel against everything that came before.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah. Yeah.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: You know, I've been wondering lately. Do you know anyone who's in a happy relationship?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Uh, yeah, sure. You know, I know happy couples. But I think they lie to each other.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Hmmph. Yeah. People can lead their life as a lie. My grandmother, she was married to this man, and I always thought she had a very simple, uncomplicated love life. But she just confessed to me that she spent her whole life dreaming about another man she was always in love with. She just accepted her fate. It's so sad. And in the same time, I love the idea that she had all those emotions and feelings [I never thought she would have had.]

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I guarantee you, it was better that way. If she'd ever got to know him, you know, I'm sure he would have disappointed her eventually.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: How do you know? You don't know them.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah, I know, I know. It's just, people have these romantic projections [they put on everything.} You know. That's not based on any kind of reality.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Romantic projections?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Oh, Mr. Romantic, up there in the Ferris wheel ('Cutsie voice'.) Oh, kiss me, the sunset, oh, it‘s so beautiful.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Oh, alright, alright, alright. Tell me about your grandmother. What were you saying about her?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: No, uh --

chapters.title: Chapter 9 : You are stardust (Kleins Cafe)

lines.text: They walk around a vehicle barricade then proceed down a cobblestone walkway lined with trees and vines.
Sitting at a cafe. A pair of friars walk by, apparently in prayer.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Hey...check these guys out. “Hey Hans, I have a confession to make. I'm not wearing any underwear underneath this thing.” “Oh really?” “Does that frighten you?” (Pauses, then turns to face Céline.) Can I tell you a secret?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Come here.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: What?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.direction: Leans all the way toward her, and kisses her on the lips.
lines.text: Come here.
They pause, looking in the direction where they hear some laughter, seeing a gypsy as she finishes reading somebody's palm.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Look at this palm-reader. She's interesting-looking, no?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Uh-oh, uh-oh.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: What, what?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: I just made eye contact.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: She's not coming over here.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yes, she is.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Oh, shit. Oh, no.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Oh my God. You want your palm read?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: No, no.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: No? Are you sure?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I'm sure.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Okay.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Hello.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Here she is.

lines.speaker: Gypsy
lines.text: Ich moechte deine hand lesen.
lines.translation: Would you like your palm read?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Uh, français, English?

lines.speaker: Gypsy
lines.direction: Takes Céline's hand, and touches it.
lines.text: Want your palm read?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah. How much is it.

lines.speaker: Gypsy
lines.text: For you, fifties. Okay?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Okay.

lines.speaker: Gypsy
lines.direction: Takes Celine’s palm, gazing and running her fingers over it.
lines.text: Oh, so, you have been on a journey, and you are stranger to this place. You, are on an adventure, you seek. An adventure in your mind. You are interested in the power of the woman, in a woman's deep strength, and creativity? You are becoming this woman. You need to resign yourself to the awkwardness of life. Only if you find peace within yourself, will you find true connection with others. (Indicates, with her head, Jesse.) That is a stranger to you?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: I guess so.

lines.speaker: Gypsy
lines.direction: Takes Jesse's hand, and looks at it only briefly.
lines.text: Oh, you will be alright. He's learning. Okay. (Claps hands.) Money. (Offers hand, awaiting payment.)

lines.speaker: Gypsy
lines.text: You are both stars, don't forget. And the stars exploded billions of years ago, to form everything that is this world. Everything we know, is stardust. So don't forget, you are stardust.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I mean, that's very nice and all, I mean, that, you know, we're all stardust, and you're becoming this great woman, I mean, but I hope you don't take that any more seriously than some horoscope in a daily syndicated newspaper.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: You, what are you talking about? I mean, she knew I was on vacation, and that we didn't know each other, and that (laughs) I was going to become this great woman.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Aw c'mon. But what was that “I am learning” bullshit? I mean, that's WAY condescending. You know? I mean, she wasn't even doing me. I mean, if opportunists like that, ever had to tell the real truth, it would put their ASSES out of business. You know? lines.text: It‘s so funny how she almost didn't notice you, you know. It's weird. I wonder why. She was, she was really wise, and intense, no? I really loved what she said, you know?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: You're so (makes gesture to give impressive of wacko)…

chapters.title: Chapter 11 : Do you believe in god? - the Church

lines.text: Jesse and Céline approach a cathedral.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Think this is open?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: I don't know, let's try it.
They cross the street to enter, as a car stops and honks at them. Inside, Céline slowly walks down the aisle.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: I was in an old church like this with my grandmother a few days ago in Budapest. Even though I reject most of the religious things, I can't help but feeling for all those people that come here lost or in pain, guilt, looking for some kind of answers. It fascinates me how a single place can join so much pain and happiness for so many generations

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: You close with your grandmother?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah. I think it‘s because I always...I always have this strange feeling that I am this very old woman laying down about to die. You know, that my life is just her memories, or something.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: That's so wild. I mean, I always think that I'm still this thirteen year old boy, you know who just doesn't really know how to be an adult, pretending to live my life, taking notes for when I'll really have to do it. Kind of like I'm in a dress rehearsal for a Junior High play.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: That's funny. Then, up there in the Ferris wheel, it was like this very old woman kissing this very young boy, right?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Hmm. Do you know anything about the Quakers, the Quaker religion?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: No, not much, no.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Well, I went to this Quaker wedding once, and it was fantastic. What they do is the couple comes in and they kneel down in front of the whole congregation, and they just stare at each other, and nobody says a word unless they feel that God moves them to speak, or say something. And then, after an hour or so of just uh, staring at each other, they're married.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: That's beautiful. I like that.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: This is a horrible story.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: What?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: It‘s not the appropriate place to tell it, but...

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: What?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Well, I was driving around with this buddy of mine, he was a big atheist, and we came to a stop, next to this homeless guy. lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: That's mean, no?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.direction: They stop and look at one another.
lines.text: Yeah uh, it‘s uh.

lines.text: Yeah, I'm sure.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Mm-hmm.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: You know, you hear so much shit about people. I always feel like the general of an army when I start dating a guy, you know, plotting my strategy and maneuverings, knowing his weak points, what would hurt him, seduce him. It's horrible. (They walk a bit.) If we were around each other all the time, what do you think would be the first thing about me that would drive you mad?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: No uh, no, no, I'm not gonna answer this question, no.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Why?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I just, I dated this girl once who, who used to always ask me that question, “What about me bugs you?” you know. And so finally I said, “Well, you know, I uh, just don't think you handle criticism too well.” She flew into a rage, and broke up with me, alright? That's a true story. All she ever really wanted to do was to have an excuse to tell me what she thought was wrong with me, you know. Is that what you want?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: What?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Something about me bugs you?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: No.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: It's alright. Tell me. What is it? What about me bugs you?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Nothing, nothing at all.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Well, if it had to be something, what would it be?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: If it had to be something, if I had to think about it, I...I kind of didn't really like this reaction back at the palm reader. You were like this rooster prick.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: “Rooster prick”?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I was a “rooster prick”?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: You were like a little boy whining because all the attention wasn't focused on him.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Alright, listen, this woman robs you blind, okay?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: You were like a little boy walking by an ice cream store, crying because his mother wouldn't buy him a milkshake or something.
A voice comes from behind.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I don't care what this woman has to say about anything.

lines.speaker: Poet
lines.text: Aeaehh, entschuldigung. Eine Frage, eine Frage. Hallo! Eine Frage. Ich moechte 'was fragen, eine Frage.
lines.translation: Um, excuse me. A question, a question. Hello! A question. I'd like to ask something, a question.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: What?

lines.speaker: Poet
lines.text: Ich moechte 'was fragen, eine Frage.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Oh, I understand a little bit, but he doesn't, I'm sorry.

lines.speaker: Poet
lines.text: Okay uh, so um, may I ask you a question?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Poet
lines.text: So, I would like to make a deal with you. I mean, instead of just asking you for money, I will ask you for a word. Yeah, You give me a word, I take the word, and then, and then I will write a poem, with the word inside. And if you like it, I mean, if you like my poem, and you feel it adds something to your life in any way, then you can pay me whatever you feel like. I will write in English, of course.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Okay.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Great, alright.

lines.speaker: Poet
lines.text: So? Pick a word.
Jesse and Céline look at each other.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Ummm...

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: A word uh...milkshake.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: “Milkshake”? Oh, good. Yeah, I was gonna say “rooster prick,” but great. (Turns to poet.) “Milkshake.”

lines.speaker: Poet
lines.text: “Milkshake”? (Pauses, as if surprised by the challenge.) Okay, milkshake.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah, right, so we'll...

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Good.
The poet begins to write in his notebook, while Jesse and Celine turn away to talk amongst themselves.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: What can I say? I like this Viennese variation of a bum.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: I like what he said about adding something to your life, no?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah. So uh, were we having our first fight back there?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: No...

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah, I think so, I think we were.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Well, even if we were a little bit, you know. Why does everyone think conflict is so bad? There's a lot of good things coming out of conflict.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah. Yeah, I guess so. I don't know, you know? I always think that if I could just accept the fact that my life was supposed to be difficult, you know, that's what's to be expected, then, I might not get so pissed off about it, and I'd just be glad when something nice happens.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Maybe that's why I'm still in school, you know. It‘s easier to have something to fight against.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah, well, we've all had such competitiveness engrained in us...
Poet finishes, and rips sheet from book.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: ...you know, I could be doing the most nothing thing, you know, I could be uh, throwing some darts, or shooting some pool, and all of a sudden, I feel it come over me, “I have got to win.”

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Is that why you tried to get me off the train? Competitiveness?
Poet stands up and approaches them.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: What do you mean?

lines.speaker: Poet
lines.text: Okay. (Hands the sheet to them.) Look at the poem.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Oh, alright. (Opens it up.)

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.direction: Takes poem from Jesse, offers it back to Poet.
lines.text: Will you read it to us?

lines.speaker: Poet
lines.text: Sure, okay. (Reads it.)
Daydream delusion.
Limousine Eyelash.
Oh, baby with your pretty face
Drop a tear in my wineglass.
Look at those big eyes
See what you mean to me.
Sweet cakes and milkshakes. (Laughs.)
I am a delusioned angel.
I am a fantasy parade.
I want you to know what I think
Don't want you to guess anymore.
You have no idea where I came from.
We have no idea where we're going
Launched in life
Like branches in the river.
Flowing downstream
Caught in the current.
I'll carry you. You'll carry me.
That's how it could be.
Don't you know me? (Poet hands poem back.)
Don't you know me by now?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Great. Thanks.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Thanks, man. (They both reach for change to give to the poet.) Uh here you go, uh…

lines.speaker: Poet
lines.text: Thanks, thank you.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Here, thank you.

lines.speaker: Poet
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah, good luck, man.

lines.speaker: Poet
lines.text: Bye.

lines.speaker: Jesse/Céline
lines.text: Bye.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: That's wonderful, no?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah, yeah.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: What?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: You know he probably didn't just write that. I mean, you know he wrote it, but he probably just plugs that word in (points his finger for emphasis), you know, whatever “milkshake”...

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: What do you mean?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.direction: Reconsidering his words, then motions with his hands as if to “back off.”
lines.text: Nothing, I love it, it was great.

lines.text: The scene opens with Jesse and Celine walking through a square surrounded by industrial-looking buildings. Some walls are covered in graffiti.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: You know what drives me crazy?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: What?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: It‘s all these people talking about how great technology is, and how it saves all this time. But, what good is saved time, if nobody uses it? If it just turns into more busy work.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Right, I mean, you never hear somebody say, "Well, you know, with uh, the time I've saved by using my word processor, I'm gonna go to a Zen monastery and hang out." I mean, you never hear that.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Time is so abstract anyway. Were you looking at this girl?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: What? What?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Nothing.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Do you want to go in here?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: What?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Do you want to go in here?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah. It‘s a club, no?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Wanna go?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Allo.

lines.text: Fifty shillings.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Fifty shillings.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Fifty shillings.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Each.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I got a hundred. Here, I got it.

lines.speaker: Céline

lines.text: Ja, das war noch nicht alles von mir, besser gesagt es kommen noch ein paar von mir.
lines.translation: Yeah, that wasn't all from me yet, I mean there's more from me to come.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: You gonna buy me a beer?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Alright.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.direction: Voice fading, as the scene changes.
lines.text: You think Ole Milwaukee's a little expensive here?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Merde! (Shit!)

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Well, um, we haven't talked about this yet, but are you dating anyone? You got a boyfriend waiting on you back in Paris, or anything like that?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: No, not right now.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.direction: He loses ball, she takes over.
lines.text: Not right…but you did?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: We broke up about six months ago.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Six months ago.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I'm sorry. I mean, I'm not that sorry. But, uh, tell me about it.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Ah, no. No, no way, I can't. It‘s really, really boring.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: C'mon, tell me about it.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Okay. I was really disappointed. I thought this one would last for a while. I mean he was very stupid, ugly, bad in bed, alcoholic, you know.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Real prize-winner.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah. (Laughs.) I was kind of giving him a favor, but he left me, saying I loved him too much, and, you know, I was blocking his artistic expression, or some shit like that, you know. But anyway, I was traumatized, and became (She loses ball. She shrugs, they switch.) and became totally obsessed with him. And so I went to see this shrink, you know, and it came out that I had written this little stupid story about this woman, trying to kill her boyfriend, and how she was gonna do it, you know, with all the intricate details of, you know, how to do it, and not get caught, And...

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: She was gonna kill her boyfriend?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah. Yeah, she was. I mean, it’s nothing I would do, but it was just some writing, you know.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Alright, no, no, I understand.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: But anyway, this stupid shrink believed everything I was telling her, and it was my first time seeing her. She said she had to call the police.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: She had to call the police?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah. She was, merde! She was totally convinced I was really gonna do it, you know, even though I'd explained to her it was just some writing, you know. She said, looking deep into my eyes, "The way you said it, I know you are going to do it, the way you said it." She was totally out of her mind. It was my first and last session.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah, so what happened then?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: I totally got over him, you know. But now I'm obsessed that he's gonna die from an accident, or you know, a thousand kilometers away, I'm gonna be the one accused. Why do you become obsessed with people you don't really like that much, you know, I mean…

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I don't know.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: So, how about you?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: What?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Are you with anyone?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Umm, it‘s funny how we managed to avoid this subject for so long, isn't it?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah, but now you have to tell me.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Well, I kind of see love as this uh, escape for two people who don't know how to be alone, you know, or uh, I mean, you know it‘s funny. People always talk about how love is this totally unselfish, giving thing, but if you think about it, you know, there's nothing more selfish.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah, I know. So, who just broke up with you?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: What?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: You sound like you've just been hurt, or something.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: No...do I?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Alright. Um, big confession, you know. I should have told you this earlier, Céline, but, you know...I didn't just come to Europe just to hang out, and read Hemingway in Paris, and shit like that, you know. I saved up my money all spring to uh, fly to Madrid, and spend the summer with my girlfriend, who has been on this...

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Your girlfriend?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: My EX-girlfriend, who has been on this asinine art history program for the last year. Anyway, I got here, right, and now we're reunited, at long last, and we went out to dinner, our first night ah, with six of her friends: Pedro, Antonio, Gonzalo, Maria, Suzie, from home, you know? She pretty much managed to avoid being alone with me for the first couple of days we were there, and I stuck around for a while, just to kind of let it really sink in that she wished I hadn't come. So I bought the cheapest flight out of Europe, this one leaving out of Vienna tomorrow, but it didn't leave for a couple of weeks. So, I bought this Eurail pass, you know? You know…you know what's the worst thing about somebody breaking up with you? It‘s when you remember how little you thought about the people you broke up with, and you realize that that is how little they're thinking about you, you know? (Loses ball.) You know, you'd like to think that you're both in all this pain, but really, they're just, “Hey, I'm glad you're gone.“ (They switch.)

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: I know. You should look at bright colors.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: What?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: That's what the shrink told me, you know. I was paying her nine-hundred francs an hour, to hear that I was a homicidal maniac, and that I could eliminate my obsession if I would concentrate on bright colours.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah, well did it work?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Well…

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Didn't help your pinball, did it?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: No. Yeah, well, you know. I haven't...I haven't killed anyone lately.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.direction: Céline gives him a sadistic look, as if to say, “Not necessarily.”
lines.text: Not lately? Well, that's good, you're cured, then.

chapters.title: Chapter 14 : The Answer must be in the attempt (The Alley)

lines.text: Jesse and Céline have resumed walking outside. We see them approaching the top of some stairs, then continuing down a quiet street.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I mean, there's these breeds of monkeys, right, and all they do is have sex, like all the time, you know? And uh, they turn out to be, like the least violent, the most peaceful, the most happy, you know, so I mean, maybe fooling around is not so bad.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Are you talking about monkeys?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yes. I'm talking about monkeys.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Ah, I thought so, yeah.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Why?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: You know, I never heard this one, but it reminds me of, like this perfect, you know, male argument to justify them fooling around.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: No, no, no. Woman monkeys are fooling around, too. (Waves his hands to defend his point.) Everybody's fooling around.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah, that's cute. (They laugh.) You know, I have this awful paranoid thought, that feminism was mostly invented by men, so they could, like, fool around a little more. You know, women, free your minds, free your bodies, sleep with me. We're all happy and free as long as I can fuck (makes a punching motion with her fist) as much as I want.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Alright, alright, alright. But maybe, maybe there's some biological things at work here. I mean, if you had an island, right, and there were ninety-nine women on the island, and only one man, in a year, you'd have the possibility of ninety-nine babies. But if you have an island with ninety-nine men, and only one woman, in a year, you'd have the possibility of only one baby. So...

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: So. You know what?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: What?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: On this island, you know, I think that there will only be, like maybe forty-three men left. Because they would kill each other, trying to fuck this poor woman, you know what I mean? And on the other island, there would be ninety-nine women, ninety-nine babies, and no more man, because they would have all gotten together, and eaten him alive.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Oh yeah?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.direction: Smiling and nodding in mock agreement.
lines.text: Yeah? Yeah? See...see, I think there's something to that. I think on some level, women don't mind the idea of destroying a man, you know. Like, I was once walking down the street with my ex-girlfriend, you know, right, and we just walked by these, like real four, kind of (twitches shoulders in a “tough guy” sort of motion) thuggy looking guys, next to a Camaro, you know, and one of 'em, sure enough, says, “Hey baby, nice ass.” You know, I mean. So, I'm like alright, “Hey, no big deal,” I'm not gonna get uptight about this, right?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah, plus, there were four of them, right?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah, exactly, there's four of them, right, but she turns around and she says, (flips the bird to the air behind him.) “Fuck you, dickheads,” and I'm like, okay, wait a minute, here, right? They're not gonna come over here and kick her ass, you know what I mean? So who just got pushed to the front line on that one? You see what I'm saying? I mean, women say they hate it if you‘re all territorial and protective, but if it suits them, then they'll tell you you're being all unmanly, or wimpy, or uh…

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: You know what? I don't think women really want to destroy men, and if, even if they want to, they don't...they don't succeed. You know what I mean? I'm sure even, you know, men are destroying women, or are able...capable of destroying women, much more than women...Well, anyway, it‘s depressing, I mean you know what?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: What? You want to stop talking about this?
Voices fade as they walk down an incline with their backs to the camera.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah. I really hate it. You know, men, women you know, it‘s, it‘s...there's no end to this, like, you know...

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: It‘s like a skipping record, you know?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Every couple's been having this conversation forever.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: And nobody's come up with anything.
The scene cuts to a belly dancer dancing to a percussionist, performing on a street corner as several people watch. Jesse and Céline approach, then Céline pulls Jesse closer to watch.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: I saw a documentary on that. It's a birth dance.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: A birth dance?

lines.speaker: Céline

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Actually...I think I decided I wanted to sleep with you when we got off the train. But now that we've talked so much, I don't know anymore.
Jesse sighs of frustration and collapses to the ground again. Celine laughs, then leans over to kiss him.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Why do we make everything so complicated?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I don't know.
They kiss again, breathing more deeply, and rolling over each other several times.

highlights.text: It’s just they are sick to death of being around themselves.
highlights.context: Oh, yeah. Yeah. I know what you mean about wishing somebody wasn't there though, It‘s just, usually, it‘s myself that I wish I could get away from. Seriously, think about this. I have never been anywhere that I haven't been. I've never had a kiss when I wasn't one of the kissers. You know, I've never, um, gone to the movies, when I wasn't there in the audience. I've never been out bowling, if I wasn't there, making some stupid joke. That's why so many people hate themselves. Seriously. It’s just they are sick to death of being around themselves. Let‘s say that you and I were together all the time, then you'd start to hate a lot of my mannerisms. The way...the way every time that we would have people over...I'd be insecure, and I'd get a little too drunk. Or...the way I tell the same stupid pseudo-intellectual story again, and again. Y'see, I've heard all those stories...So of course I'm sick of myself. But being with you...it‘s made me feel like I was somebody else. I mean the only other way to lose yourself like that is...you know, dancing...or alcohol...or drugs or stuff like that.
highlights.speaker: Jesse

highlights.text: Why do we make everything so complicated?
highlights.context: Why do we make everything so complicated?
highlights.speaker: Céline

highlights.context: I don't know.
highlights.speaker: Jesse

chapters.title: Chapter 20 : I’m gonna take your picture - the harpsichordist

lines.text: In park...sun is up, birds are chirping. Scene cuts to city, where Jesse and Celine are walking along a street. Harpsichord music plays in the background.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: What's the first thing you'll do when you get back to Paris?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Call my parents.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: What about you?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I don't know...I'll probably go pick up my dog. He's still with a friend of mine.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: You have a dog?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: I love dogs.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: You do?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Oh shit!

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: What?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Oh, I don't know. We're back in real time.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: I know. I hate that.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.direction: Notices sound, and walks towards it.
lines.text: What is that?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Sounds like a harpsichord.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Check that out.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Somebody’s playing.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: That’s cool.
They look into basement window, where there is a man playing a harpsichord.
Jesse pulls Céline to the side of the window.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Can we dance to the harpsichord?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Of course.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.direction: Looking at her. He stops her dancing.
lines.text: Oh, wow.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: What?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I'm gonna take your picture (puts her at arms length, and stares) so I never forget you...or...or all this.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Okay. Me, too.
She stops and stares at him too. He leans over and they kiss. Eventually, they stop, and walk away holding hands.

chapters.title: Chapter 21 : The years shall run like rabbits - the statue

lines.text: Camera shows various views of the landmarks of Vienna, stopping at a statue in a square, upon which Jesse sits while Céline lies with her head on his lap, eyes closed.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: “The years shall run like rabbits.“

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.direction: Opens her eyes and looks up at him.
lines.text: What?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Nothing, nothing. I have this, uh, recording of Dylan Thomas, reading a W.H.Auden poem. He's got a great voice. Just it's like, uh...

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: What, what?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: (Starts with throaty voice again.)
All the clocks in the city
Began to whir, and chime
Oh, let not time deceive you
You cannot conquer time.
In headaches and in worry
Vaguely life leaks away.
And time will have its fancy
Tomorrow or today.
(Back to regular voice.) Something like that.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.direction: They stop and stare for a while.
lines.text: That‘s good. (Pauses.) When you talked earlier about after a few years, how a couple begin to hate each other...by anticipating their reactions...or getting tired of their mannerisms. I think it would be the opposite for me. I think I can really fall in love when I know everything about someone. The way he's gonna part his hair...which shirt he's gonna wear that day...knowing the exact story he'd tell in a given situation. I'm sure that's when I know I'm really in love.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Hey, guess what?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: What?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: We didn't go to those guys' play.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Play?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: With the cow?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah, we didn't. Oh no, we missed it. (Sigh.)

chapters.title: Chapter 22 : Goodbye - Goodbye - Au Revoir - Later

lines.text: In train station. Jesse and Céline walk side by side, together holding her bag between them. Voice over loudspeaker makes an inaudible announcement.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Okay, you know what bus to take to the airport?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah, yeah. No problem.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.direction: Pointing to a coach. They stop.
lines.text: I should get on this one

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Right here? You wanna to get on there?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Alright. Um...

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Okay. I guess this is it, no?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.direction: Breathing heavy, like after workout or from anxiety.
lines.text: Yeah. Um, I really, (A couple of deep breaths.) I, uh, I... I mean, you know what I mean.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah, I know what -- I, uh. Yeha, My...Have a great life. Have fun with everything you're gonna do. Work hard...

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah. Good luck with school, and all that.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Okay.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: I hate this.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Me too. The train is about to leave.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah.
They kiss, hug. They stop, and from this point on their voices are rushed.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Listen. Listen. You know all this bullshit we're talking about...about not seeing each other again? I don't want to do that.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: I don't want to do that either.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: You don't?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: I waited for you to say it.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Well, why didn't you say something?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: I was afraid you didn't wanna see me.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Alright, alright, well look. Listen, listen. What-d...what-d...What do you wanna do?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Maybe... maybe we should meet here, in five years or something.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Alright, alright. Five years. (Disapprovingly.) Five years? That's a long time.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yes. It‘s awful. It‘s like a sociological experiment. How about one year?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: One year. Alright, alright.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: One year.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: How about six months?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Six months?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: It‘s gonna be freezing.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Yeah?

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Who cares? We come here, we go somewhere else.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Okay. Okay. Uh, six months from now, or last night?

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Um...Last night. Six months from last night, which was...June 16th. So...track nine, six months from now at six o'clock, at night.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Dece--December.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: December, yeah, right. Now listen, it‘s a train ride for you, but I got to fly all the way here. But I'm gonna be here.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Okay, me too.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Alright.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: And we won‘t call...or write or...

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Na...

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Na.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: It‘s depressing.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Yeah, okay.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Alright. (They kiss.) Alright, your train's gonna leave. Say goodbye.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Bye.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Goodbye.

lines.speaker: Céline
lines.text: Au revoir.

lines.speaker: Jesse
lines.text: Later.
They kiss again, and he helps her onto the train. The whistle blows, and the train leaves.

highlights.text: I waited for you to say it.
highlights.context: I waited for you to say it.
highlights.speaker: Céline

chapters.title: Chapter 23 : Ending montage and Closing Credits

lines.text: We see Celine, alone as she enters a passenger compartment on the train. We see Jesse, alone as he takes the escalator in the train station, then later as he rides the bus to the airport.
“Andante” From Sonata For Viola Da Gamba In G Major by Bach plays in the background as the closing montage begins to roll
